metadata.title: Asymptotic Parallel Solver in Compressible DNS Code

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This paper does not use any ILSA/OECD student micro-data, plausible values, or survey sampling. The study is a computational-methods paper that develops and benchmarks an asymptotic parallel linear solver within a direct numerical simulation (DNS) code for compressible isothermal turbulence. As a result, there are no sampling weights, replicate weights, or complex survey design elements to apply. Any weighting discussion is not applicable because the “data” are simulated fields on a numerical grid rather than a probability sample of students.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the study does not analyze ILSA achievement outcomes (e.g., PISA/TIMSS/PIRLS cognitive scores) and instead evaluates numerical solvers and DNS performance on simulated physical fields. Missing-data handling is not reported because there is no student-level dataset with missing questionnaire/test responses; the computations are deterministic given the numerical setup and grid resolution.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Not applicable: the paper uses numerical simulations on a 3D Cartesian grid with periodic boundary conditions. The “sample” is defined by simulation parameters (e.g., grid size N^3, subdomain decomposition layout npx×npy×npz, and solver choice based on M≥64), not by an empirical participant sample.

data.outcome_summary: This paper proposes an asymptotic parallel linear solver for reduced matrices arising from an eighth-order compact finite-difference scheme used inside a direct numerical simulation (DNS) code for compressible isothermal turbulence. The computational domain is a cube with periodic boundary conditions, discretized on a uniform N×N×N grid; spatial derivatives are computed using CD8 for convection terms and FD8 for viscous terms. The solver is applied when the number of grid points per subdomain in a Cartesian direction satisfies M≥64, otherwise a normal Mattor-based parallel solver is used. Performance is evaluated on the SX-Aurora TSUBASA vector supercomputer using MPI cuboid decomposition and halo exchange. Reported results include a 1.7× speedup of the optimized code versus the original for a DNS with 2048^3 grid points, and an approximately 4-fold speedup of the asymptotic solver compared to the Mattor solver for a single solver call. The study also reports excellent weak scalability, with communication overhead increasing for larger MPI decompositions but remaining manageable.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse with respect to ILSA-style fields because the provided article text is not an educational large-scale assessment study. It is a computational science paper focused on numerical linear solvers and DNS performance, with no student sampling, no questionnaire variables, and no predictive modeling of educational outcomes. Therefore, fields such as countries, sample sizes, plausible values, missing-data handling, and ML techniques are not meaningful in this context.
